Ugraśravā, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa, a sūta versed in the Purāṇas, came once to the twelve-year sacrificial session of Śaunaka, lord of the kula, in the Naimiṣa forest.
The son of the sūta approached the brahmarṣis who were seated there, those of sharpened vows, bowing humbly before them.
When he arrived at that hermitage, the ascetics dwelling in the Naimiṣa forest gathered around him, eager to hear his wondrous tales.
Having saluted all those sages with palms joined, he enquired after the progress of their austerities, and was in turn warmly greeted by those good men.
When all the ascetics had taken their seats, Lomaharṣaṇi humbly took the seat that had been indicated for him.
Seeing him comfortably seated and rested, a certain ṛṣi then asked him a question, setting the conversation in motion.

Aṣṭaka said: How many kinds of sages are there, and how many kinds of silence are there? Tell us this — we wish to hear.
Yayāti said: He for whom the village lies behind while dwelling in the forest, or for whom the forest lies behind while dwelling in the village — that man may be called a sage, O lord of the people.
Aṣṭaka said: How is it that when one dwells in the forest the village comes to lie behind, and how is it that when dwelling in the village the forest comes to lie behind?
Yayāti said: He who would be a forest-dwelling sage should not make use of village things; in that way, even while dwelling in the forest, the village comes to lie behind him.
Without fire, without a fixed dwelling, moving without clan affiliations, the sage should desire clothing only to the extent of a loincloth for covering.

'Or, O king, let the death of Bhīmasena be arranged through men skilled in stratagems, working in secret — for he is the greatest in strength among them.
'For when he has been slain, O king, their enthusiasm will be crushed, their energy broken — they will no longer strive for the kingdom. He is indeed their chief support.
'For Arjuna is invincible in battle when Vṛkodara is guarding his back. Without Phalguna, in battle Rādheya does not even reach his feet.
'Knowing their great weakness without Bhīmasena, and knowing us to be the stronger party, they who are weaker will not prevail against us.
'When the sons of Pṛthā have come here and are subject to our authority, O king, we shall proceed as we see fit to crush them.
'Or alternatively let each son of Kuntī there be seduced by beautiful women, and then let Kṛṣṇā become disillusioned with them.

Then Gāndhārī, wasted by grief, spoke righteously to the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of men, whose heart was swayed by love for his son:
"When Duryodhana was born, the great-minded Vidura declared: 'This one, the defiler of the family, should rightly be sent to the other world.'
For he cried out like a jackal the very moment he was born, O Bhārata — truly this is the end of this family; understand that, O Kurus.
O lord, do not follow the counsel of these foolish and ill-bred boys; do not yourself become the cause of this terrible destruction of the family.
Who would demolish a built dam? Who would blow upon a fire that is extinguished? Who, O Bhārata, would provoke the Pārthas who have been held in check by peace?
O Ajamīḍha, I remind you now as you yourself remember: scripture does not rule over the evil-minded — for their good or otherwise.

Having bathed there and having worshipped Śūlapāṇi, the bearer of the bull-banner, with a soul purified of all sins, one would proceed to the highest state.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent Phalakirvana; where the gods, O king, ever resorting to Phalakirvana, perform great austerities for many thousands of years.
A man having bathed in the Dṛṣadvatī and having gratified the gods obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma and the Atirātra, O Bhārata.
And having bathed at the tirtha of all the gods, O best of Bhāratas, a man, O king of kings, obtains the fruit of a thousand cows.
A man having bathed at Panikhata and having gratified the gods obtains the Rājasūya sacrifice and goes to the world of the sages.
Then one should go, O king of kings, to the excellent tirtha of Miśraka; there the tirthas have been mixed together, O king of kings, by the great soul —

Thus Vṛkodara lamented greatly in various ways, bound by the serpent's coils and unable to stir.
Meanwhile Yudhiṣṭhira, son of Kuntī, became uneasy of mind, pondering the dreadful and ill-omened portents he was witnessing.
For a jackal, standing to the south in the blazing quarter, terrified, was uttering a fierce and inauspicious howl near that hermitage.
A quail, hideous to behold, with one wing, one eye, and one foot, was seen vomiting blood toward the sun, crying with ill omens.
A harsh and violent wind blew, dragging gravel along, and all the cries of beasts and birds went in the inauspicious direction.
A black crow behind him cawed again and again "Go, go!" and his right arm throbbed repeatedly.
His heart and left foot twitched, and an inauspicious change came over his left eye.

"Gandharvas and apsaras, O auspicious one, O fair-thighed one, always attend upon me when I drink, even as they do my brother."
"I am the son of the brahmin sage Viśravas himself; my fame is renowned as the fifth among the guardians of the worlds."
"Divine foods to eat and drink of all varieties are mine just as they are Indra's, O passionate one."
"Let the evil karma of forest-dwelling be exhausted for you; be my wife, O beautiful-hipped one, even as Mandodarī is."
Thus addressed by him, the daughter of Videha, her face beautiful, turned away and placing a blade of grass between herself and him, spoke to that night-wanderer.
That young woman of exquisitely beautiful thighs, inauspicious in his sight, her two breasts struck together while she continuously rained tears from her eyes—the daughter of Videha, who holds her husband as her god, spoke this word to that wretch.

If the bull of the Kurus should make peace through righteous means, then the great destruction of Kurus and Pāṇḍavas as brothers will not come to pass.
But if the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, filled with pride and delusion, should refuse, then after sending to the others, you may summon us in turn.
Then that dull-witted Duryodhana, foolish together with his ministers and kinsmen, will meet his end when the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow is enraged.
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Virāṭa, lord of the earth, having duly honoured the Vārṣṇeya, sent him homeward together with his retinue and kinsmen.
When Kṛṣṇa had departed for Dvārakā, Yudhiṣṭhira and his brothers, along with king Virāṭa lord of the earth, made all preparations for war.
Then Virāṭa together with his kinsmen, and king Drupada lord of the earth, sent messengers to all the rulers of the land.

The son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra hopes for sovereign rule of the earth without a rival; in him peace alone is not to be found — he considers what he seeks as already bound and delivered.
This earth, ripened by time, is ready to be overturned; all warriors of the earth, eager to fight for Duryodhana's sake against the Pāṇḍavas, have gathered, and kings along with their protectors.
All these kings who formerly had enmity with you, O Kṛṣṇa, and who had their essence taken away by you — out of dread of you they have joined the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; those heroes are firmly united together with Karṇa.
All those warriors, who have abandoned themselves along with Duryodhana and are set loose to fight the Pāṇḍavas — O hero of the Dāśārha clan, it is not my wish that you enter into their midst.

In Kṛttikā, the first of mansions, a fierce planet, blazing and stealing away forms with its glare, stands like a smoking comet.
Through all three of the earlier mansions, O lord of peoples, Budha (Mercury) repeatedly speeds, engendering exceedingly great fear.
A fourteenth-day moon, a fifteenth-day moon, and once even a sixteenth I have known; but this new moon falling on a thirteenth day I have never known before.
Both moon and sun eclipsed within a single month, on the thirteenth day and out of their proper season — these two seizures shall bring the peoples to ruin.
All the quarters are wrapped in dust, with showers of grit on every side; and dreadful portent-clouds rain down blood in the night.
Again, on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, at midnight, there came a fierce and most terrible rain of flesh, whereat the rākṣasas glutted themselves unsated.

The son of Hiḍimbā, foremost of the Rākṣasas, rushed with fury upon the great archer of Prāgjyotiṣa, as one frenzied elephant charges another in rut.
Then, O king, the Rākṣasa Alambusa, full of wrath, charged in battle against Sātyaki, hard to overcome in war, together with his troops.
Bhūriśravas, intent in the fight, did battle with Dhṛṣṭaketu, while Yudhiṣṭhira the son of Dharma engaged King Śrutāyus.
Cekitāna in the battle fought against Kṛpa; the rest, intent upon it, advanced against Bhīma, that mighty chariot-warrior.
Then kings by the thousands surrounded Dhanaṃjaya, their hands grasping spears, lances, iron arrows, maces, and bludgeons.
Then Arjuna, exceedingly wrathful, spoke thus to the descendant of Vṛṣṇi: "Behold, O Mādhava, the armies of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son drawn up for battle by the great-souled son of Gaṅgā, who knows the art of arrays.

Those who watched Kṛpa and the Vṛṣṇi fighting, brilliant in combat, became so engrossed in the battle that they marked no other doings.
The son of Somadatta beset King Maṇimat, the unwearied, as he came on, thus increasing Droṇa's glory.
He, swiftly cutting away the son of Somadatta's bow and banner, then cast down his pennon, his driver, and his parasol from the chariot.
Then the foe-slayer whose ensign was the sacrificial post, leaping swiftly from his chariot, cut him to pieces — horses, driver, banner, and car — with his excellent sword.
And mounting his own chariot, taking up another bow, himself reining his horses, O king, he shattered the army of the Pāṇḍavas.
With pestles, mallets, discs, slings, and battle-axes, with dust and wind and fire and water, with ashes, clods, grass, and trees —

Droṇa of mighty strength, having slain his horses and his charioteer, then assailed him with twenty-five arrows.
Deprived of his car and bereft of his bow, the king of the Cedis too, enraged in the fray, hurled his mace toward the chariot of the son of Bharadvāja.
That mace, rushing down in sudden onset—of terrible form and fearsome, heavy, made of iron and adorned with gold—the son of Bharadvāja brought to the ground with many thousands of arrows.
That mace, struck down by the son of Bharadvāja, fell to the earth, decked with red garlands and cloth, like a star falling from the floor of heaven.
Seeing his mace struck down, the wrathful Dhṛṣṭaketu swiftly let fly a lance and a gold-gleaming spear.
But Droṇa, deft of hand and of mighty strength, cleaving the lance with three arrows in that great battle, sundered the spear at once.

That mighty archer, deeply wounded, as if bewildered in the fray, with a keen-edged broad-headed shaft cut asunder his great bow.
And whatever arrow he sent, and his bows besides, O lord of peoples, the unassailable one cut them all to pieces, and his mace and his sword as well.
Then the scorcher of foes, enraged, pierced the wrathful-looking Dhṛṣṭadyumna with nine keen arrows that bring life to its end.
That great chariot-warrior of measureless soul mingled the horses of Dhṛṣṭadyumna's car with the horses of his own, and loosed the Brāhma weapon.
Thus mingled, those swift steeds, fleet as the wind, shone splendidly—some dove-colored, some red, O bull of the Bhāratas.
As thundering clouds charged with lightning at the coming of the rains, so, O great king, they shone, intermingled at the head of the battle.

All things, moving and unmoving, broke into cries of woe, seeing the two protectors of all that moves and is still covered over with arrows.
And the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas gathered together from every side, anxiously wondering whether the welfare of the worlds might yet be preserved this day.
Never before, O king, had I beheld such prowess as arose in the son of Droṇa as he covered the two Kṛṣṇas over with arrows.
The twang of the son of Droṇa's bow, terrifying his foes in the battle, I heard again and again, O king, like the roaring of a lion.
And his bowstring, as he ranged through the battle shooting to left and right, became like lightning flashing in the midst of the clouds.
Then the Pāṇḍava, swift of action and firm of hand though he was, fell into utter bewilderment and gazed upon the son of Droṇa.

"Yet without the king's own entry, how is it that you have come here? Tell me the whole reason of this in full."
Yuyutsu said: "When Śakuni was slain, dear sir, with his kinsmen, sons, and relations, then King Duryodhana, with but the remnant of his retinue left, abandoned his own horse and, turning eastward, fled in fear."
"When the king had withdrawn from the encampment of the host, all the people, distraught with fear, fled toward the city."
"Then the keepers of the women, mounting upon the carriages the consorts of the king and of all his brothers, fled in fear."
"Then I, having taken leave of the king together with Keśava, entered Hāstinapura, to guard against the world's reproach."
Hearing these words spoken by the son of the vaiśya woman, and knowing them timely, Vidura, knower of all that is right, of immeasurable soul, honored the eloquent Yuyutsu.

Beside Droṇa, slain by the son of Drupada, O slayer of Madhu, Kṛpī sits in piteous grief, her senses overborne by sorrow.
Behold her, weeping and anguished, her hair unbound, her face cast down, attending upon her slain husband Droṇa, best of those who bear arms.
Beside Droṇa, his armor pierced through by the arrows of Dhṛṣṭadyumna, O Keśava, sits she upon the field, her hair matted, faithful and chaste.
And Kṛpī, delicate and renowned, stricken and forlorn, strives to perform the funeral rites of her lord slain in battle.
Bringing the sacred fires as the rite ordains and kindling the pyre on every side, the chanters of the Sāman lay Droṇa upon it and sing the three Sāman melodies.
And these matted-haired celibate students heap the pyre with bows, with spears, and with the framework-seats of chariots, O Mādhava.

This grievous calamity of yours is the inner kind, born of your own deeds; for all these troubles spring from Akrūra and the Bhojas and follow in their train.
For the sake of gain, or out of desire, or through Dvāravatī, or even from loathing, the sovereignty you yourself had won was made over to others.
Now that lordship has struck root, has gained renown, and has won its supporters; it cannot be taken back again by you, any more than food once vomited up.
The kingdom of Babhru and Ugrasena can in no way be regained — out of fear of a split among the kinsmen, O Kṛṣṇa, and least of all by you.
And if it should be accomplished by great effort, after performing a most arduous deed, it would bring vast ruin and expense, or else destruction would come once again.
With a weapon not of iron, soft, yet cleaving to the very heart, draw out the tongue of all of them, stroking and soothing them again and again.

For the man of wealth, victorious, is able to honor the highest dharma and to pursue desire — both beyond the reach of those who have not mastered themselves.
Dharma and kāma are but the limbs of artha — so says the sacred word; for once wealth is secured, these two are brought to their fulfillment.
For the man whose fortune has risen, even those of nobler birth attend upon him without ceasing, as living creatures attend upon Brahmā.
Bearing matted locks and deerskins, self-disciplined, smeared with mud, their senses conquered, shaven, casting off the sacred thread — even such men dwell apart, each a seeker of gain.
Others, robed in ochre, bearded, well-cloaked in modesty, learned and serene, freed of all possessions —
some among them seek gain, others long for heaven, and some uphold the customs of their line — each following his own road.

Then once that great ascetic, taking no food and feeding on air alone, stood still as a log, unmoved, and stirred not at all.
While he stood thus, become like a tree-stump, motionless, O Bhārata—a pair of kuliṅga sparrows, O king, made a nest upon his head.
That compassionate brahmin-seer watched the mated pair as they fashioned their little nest there in his matted locks with strands of grass.
And since that great ascetic, become like a stump, stirred not at all, the two birds, grown wholly trusting, dwelt there in ease.
Then, when the rains had passed and the autumn season had come, the pair, made trusting and overcome by desire, after the manner ordained of Prajāpati,
those two skyfarers, O king, let fall their eggs upon his head; and that splendid brahmin of strict vows became aware of them.

Brahmā, Sthāṇu, Manu, Dakṣa, Bhṛgu, Dharma, Tapas, Dama, Marīci, Aṅgiras and Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Vasiṣṭha and Parameṣṭhin, Vivasvat and Soma, he who is called Kardama, and Krodha and Vikrīta —
twenty-one in number arose, and these are remembered as the Lords of Creatures; they honour the eternal bound of that god.
Knowing truly the rites to the gods and to the fathers as ever belonging to That, the best of the twice-born thereby come to know the things that are attained within the Self.
Whatever embodied beings, even those dwelling in heaven, bow down to That, they by its grace go to the goal whose fruit has been appointed by it.
Those who are freed of the seventeen attributes and of works as well, and have cast off the fifteen parts — these, it is determined, are the liberated.

have fallen into the condition of degraded men through the absence of brahmans. Better is defeat at their hands than victory, O best of the victorious.
Even one who should slay all this world—there is nothing equal to slaying a brahman; the killing of a brahman is a grievous sin, so say the supreme seers.
Reviling of the twice-born must never be listened to under any circumstance. Either let a man sit silent with face bowed down, or let him rise and walk away.
There is none born, nor to be born, upon this earth, who by setting himself against the brāhmaṇas could dare to live in ease.
Hard to seize with the fist is the wind, hard to touch with the hand is the moon, hard to bear upon the head is the earth—and hard to conquer upon this world are the brāhmaṇas.
Bhīṣma said: The brāhmaṇas, ever and always, one should honor with the utmost zeal, for they have Soma for their king and are the masters of joy and sorrow.

There for a thousand aeons he rejoices in the company of his beloveds, and feeds on the nectar-draught, supreme and like the elixir of immortality.
He who takes a single meal on the nineteenth day, ever for twelve months, beholds the seven worlds.
He gains a supreme abode, attended by hosts of apsarases, and a chariot bright as the sun, hymned by the gandharvas.
There, freed from all fever of grief, he rejoices with the fairest women of the immortals, clad in heavenly raiment and full of splendor, for a hundred myriads of years.
And he who takes a single meal when the twentieth day is full, ever for twelve months, speaking truth and steadfast in his vow,
eating no flesh, observing chastity, devoted to the welfare of all beings, attains the vast and heavenly worlds of the Ādityas.

Honoring guests in due season, he should also offer them shelter, sustaining himself on fruits, leaves, lowly roots, and wild millet.
He should partake, in due order and according to his consecration and unwearied, of flowing water, of air, and of all that the forest yields, down to grass.
With roots, fruits, and the alms he has gathered he should honor a guest who comes; whatever be his own food, from that he should ever give alms, unwearied.
Serving the gods and guests first, he should always eat with restrained speech, his mind unwavering, eating lightly, his refuge in the gods.
Self-controlled, friendly, endowed with patience, wearing his hair and beard, offering oblations, given to the study of scripture, and devoted to truth and righteousness—
having renounced care of the body, ever skillful, abiding in the forest and composed—thus yoked, the forest-dweller with senses subdued shall win heaven.

Dionysus:
I, the son of Zeus, have come to this land of the Thebans—Dionysus, whom once Semele, Kadmos’ daughter, bore, delivered by a lightning-bearing flame. And having taken a mortal form instead of a god’s,
I am here at the fountains of Dirke and the water of Ismenus. And I see the tomb of my thunder-stricken mother here near the palace, and the remnants of her house, smouldering with the still living flame of Zeus’ fire, the everlasting insult of Hera against my mother.
I praise Kadmos, who has made this place hallowed, the shrine of his daughter; and I have covered it all around with the cluster-bearing leaf of the vine.
I have left the wealthy lands of the Lydians and Phrygians, the sun-parched plains of the Persians, and the Bactrian walls, and have passed over the wintry land of the Medes, and blessed Arabia, and all of Asia which lies along the coast of the salt sea with its beautifully-towered cities full of Hellenes and barbarians mingled together;

But, you women who have left Tmolus, the bulwark of Lydia, my sacred band, whom I have brought from among the barbarians as assistants and companions to me, take your drums, native instruments of the city of the Phrygians, the invention of mother Rhea and myself, and going about this palace of Pentheus beat them, so that Kadmos’ city may see. I myself will go to the folds of Kithairon, where the Bacchae are, to share in their dances.
Chorus:
From the land of Asia, having left sacred Tmolus, I am swift to perform for Bromius my sweet labor and toil easily borne, celebrating the god Bacchus. Who is in the way? Who is in the way? Who? Let him get out of the way indoors, and let everyone keep his mouth pure, speaking propitious things. For I will celebrate Dionysus with hymns according to eternal custom.

nearby, raving Satyrs were fulfilling the rites of the mother goddess, and they joined it to the dances of the biennial festivals, in which Dionysus rejoices.
Chorus:
He is sweet in the mountains, whenever after the running dance he falls on the ground, wearing the sacred garment of fawn skin, hunting the blood of the slain goat, a raw-eaten delight, rushing to the
Phrygian, the Lydian mountains, and the leader of the dance is Bromius, evoe! The plain flows with milk, it flows with wine, it flows with the nectar of bees.
The Bacchic one, raising the flaming torch of pine on his thyrsos, like the smoke of Syrian incense, darts about, arousing the wanderers with his racing and dancing, agitating them with his shouts, casting his rich locks into the air. And among the Maenad cries his voice rings deep: Go, Bacchae, go, Bacchae, with the luxury of Tmolus that flows with gold, sing of Dionysus, beneath the heavy beat of drums, celebrating in delight the god of delight with Phrygian shouts and cries, when the sweet-sounding sacred pipe sounds a sacred playful tune suited to the wanderers, to the mountain, to the mountain! And the Bacchante, rejoicing like a foal with its grazing mother, rouses her swift foot in a gamboling dance.

Pentheus:
I happened to be at a distance from this land, when I heard of strange evils throughout this city, that the women have left our homes in contrived Bacchic rites, and rush about in the shadowy mountains, honoring with dances this new deity Dionysus, whoever he is. I hear that mixing-bowls stand full in the midst of their assemblies, and that they each creep off different ways into secrecy to serve the beds of men, on the pretext that they are Maenads worshipping;
but they consider Aphrodite before Bacchus.
As many of them as I have caught, servants keep in the public strongholds with their hands bound, and as many as are absent I will hunt from the mountains,
And having bound them in iron fetters, I will soon stop them from this ill-working revelry. And they say that some stranger has come, a sorcerer, a conjuror from the Lydian land, fragrant in hair with golden curls, having in his eyes the wine-dark graces of Aphrodite. He is with the young girls day and night, alluring them with joyful mysteries. If I catch him within this house,

And do you laugh at him, because he was sewn up in Zeus’ thigh? I will teach you that this is well: when Zeus snatched him out of the lighting-flame, and led the child as a god to Olympus,
Hera wished to banish him from the sky, but Zeus, as a god, had a counter-contrivance. Having broken a part of the air which surrounds the earth, he gave this to Hera as a pledge protecting the real Dionysus from her hostility. But in time, mortals say that he was nourished in the thigh of Zeus, changing the word, because a god he had served as a hostage for the goddess Hera, and composing the story.
But this god is a prophet—for Bacchic revelry and madness have in them much prophetic skill.
For whenever the god enters a body in full force, he makes the frantic to foretell the future. He also possesses a share of Ares’ nature. For terror sometimes flutters an army under arms and in its ranks before it even touches a spear;

Pentheus:
Don’t lay a hand on me! Go off and hold your revels, but don’t wipe your foolishness off on me. I will seek the punishment of this teacher of your folly. Let someone go quickly to the seat where he watches the flights of birds, upset and overturn it with levers, turning everything upside down;
and release his garlands to the winds and storms. In this way I will especially wound him. And some of you hunt throughout the city for this effeminate stranger, who introduces a new disease to women and pollutes our beds.
If you catch him, bring him here bound, so that he might suffer as punishment a death by stoning, having seen a bitter Bacchic revelry in Thebes.
Teiresias:
O wretched man, how little you know what you are saying! You are mad now, and even before you were out of your wits.

He remained still, making my work easy, and I in shame said: Stranger, I do not lead you away willingly, but by order of Pentheus, who sent me.
And the Bacchae whom you shut up, whom you carried off and bound in the chains of the public prison, are set loose and gone, and are gamboling in the meadows, invoking Bromius as their god. Of their own accord, the chains were loosed from their feet and keys opened the doors without human hand. This man has come to Thebes full of many wonders. You must take care of the rest.
Pentheus:
Release his hands, for caught in the nets he is not so swift as to escape me. But your body is not ill-formed, stranger, for women’s purposes, for which reason you have come to Thebes.
For your hair is long, not through wrestling, scattered over your cheeks, full of desire; and you have a white skin from careful preparation, hunting after Aphrodite by your beauty not exposed to strokes of the sun, but beneath the shade.

Are you saying that you saw clearly what the god was like?
Dionysus:
He was as he chose; I did not order this.
Pentheus:
Again you diverted my question well, speaking mere nonsense.
Dionysus:
One will seem to be foolish if he speaks wisely to an ignorant man.
Pentheus:
Did you come here first, bringing the god?
Dionysus:
All the barbarians celebrate these rites.
Pentheus:
Yes, for they are far more foolish than Hellenes.
Dionysus:
In this at any rate they are wiser; but their laws are different.
Pentheus:

Where is he? He is not visible to my eyes.
Dionysus:
Near me; but you, being impious, do not see him.
Pentheus:
To attendants
Seize him; he insults me and Thebes!
Dionysus:
I warn you not to bind me, since I am in my senses and you are not.
Pentheus:
And I, more masterful than you, bid them to bind you.
Dionysus:
You do not know why you live, or what you are doing, or who you are.
Pentheus:
I am Pentheus, son of Echion and Agave.
Dionysus:
You are well-suited to be miserable in your name.

Chorus:
Io! Io! Master, master! Come now to our company, Bromius.
Dionysus:
Shake the world’s plain, lady Earthquake!
Chorus:
Oh! Oh! Soon the palace of Pentheus will be shaken in ruin.
—Dionysus is in the halls.
Revere him.
—We revere him!
—Did you see these stone lintels on the pillars falling apart? Bromius cries out in victory indoors.
Dionysus:
Light the fiery lamp of lightning!
Burn, burn Pentheus’ home!
Chorus:
Oh! Oh! Do you not see the the fire, do you not perceive, about the sacred tomb of Semele, the flame that Zeus’ thunderbolt left?
Cast on the ground your trembling bodies, Maenads, cast them down, for our lord, Zeus’ son, is coming against this palace, turning everything upside down.

Enter Pentheus
Pentheus:
I have suffered terrible things; the stranger, who was recently constrained in bonds, has escaped me. Ah!
Here is the man. What is this? How do you appear in front of my house, having come out?
Dionysus:
Stop, and put a stop to your anger.
Pentheus:
How have you escaped your chains and come outside?
Dionysus:
Did I not say—or did you not hear—that some one would deliver me?
Pentheus:
